findings.summary: The epoch decision ADR-0042's amendment forwarded to this row is answered in a // comment in SubscriptionEvent and in the backlog cell, but NOT in ADR-0043: the record never names the sentinel/special-case question, never says the slot is not special-cased, and never records that the constructor refuses grant + SESSION_EPOCH_ABSENT
findings.detail: ADR-0042 lines 211-220 state the question verbatim -- 'either a v3 body carries the sentinel, re-opening the in-band collision round 1 blocked on, or the slot is special-cased ... Deciding that is part of adding the field, not after it' -- and ADR-0043 is the record that owns it. What ADR-0043 says is 'A grant implies a session epoch, so the three shapes differ by one field each' (Consequences, first paragraph), which is a statement about LAYOUT. The answer to the forwarded question (a v3 body always carries a real epoch, 0 in that slot stays the sentinel, and the pair is refused at construction rather than encoded) appears only at SubscriptionEvent.java:440-455 and in the backlog cell. The Consequences section does record the sibling refusal ('A range without a grant is refused in the constructor') in exactly the form the epoch refusal is missing from, which is what makes the omission visible rather than stylistic. Code verified: the guard exists and is correct, and encode's `carriesGrant ||` in `carriesSessionEpoch` is now unreachable on its own -- the invariant lives in two places, one of which the ADR documents in neither.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.x appends the next optional field at VERSION_4 and follows ADR-0042's amendment forward to ADR-0043 for the precedent. The record says only 'v3 is v2 plus the grant'; it does not say that 0 in the epoch slot is still the sentinel and that an encoder must never stamp a version whose epoch slot cannot hold a real value. The author writes `carriesX || sessionEpoch != ABSENT` exactly as encode already does, omits the constructor refusal because nothing told them one was needed, and reproduces round 1's blocking defect verbatim: encode stamps VERSION_4, writes 0 into the epoch slot, decode's `(version == V2 || version == V3 || version == V4) && sessionEpoch == ABSENT` throws, and the ingester records a push every consumer rejects.

findings.summary: The corrected cost claim checks out on its numbers and its direction, but 'a reader given coordinates needs ZERO directory reads' is true only while every segment is CODEC_NONE: codecFlags lives per run in the DIRECTORY, so a ranged GET that skips the directory cannot decompress the run it fetched -- and ADR-0043 keeps `codec` off the event in the same section
findings.detail: VERIFIED FIRST, because the correction was the thing to check: (a) the ~400 figure is ADR-0042 lines 186-188 verbatim ('A node holding ~400 streams in one 8 MiB segment therefore receives ~400 events naming the same segmentKey'), so the citation is honest; (b) a range-scoped grant genuinely cannot be shared across runs -- the signature covers the range, so 400 runs need 400 signatures and 400 GETs, a rate in shards-per-node, and the inverted round-1 claim really did invert at K>=2; (c) 'one ranged GET per (node, segment) instead of one GET plus a directory read' is consistent with ADR-0042 lines 131-138 and with SPEC criterion 9's 2-GETs-per-segment accounting, and the saving is per (node, segment) as stated. So the correction is right. What is left unstated: SegmentFormat.java:17 and research doc 01 section 3 put `u32 codecFlags` in the RunEntry, i.e. in the directory, while DATA carries only `[u32 uncompressedLen][u32 crc32c][records]` -- no codec id. A consumer given byteStart/byteLen and nothing else therefore cannot decode a compressed run, so 'zero directory reads' holds only because CODEC_NONE is currently the only codec in the tree (SegmentFormat.java:69, 'M2 adds codecs'; SegmentWriter.java:109 writes it unconditionally; nothing reads codecFlags back). The fix is one clause: the single ranged GET must span the directory too -- which is constructible, since cost.md R7 puts headerLen in the KEY, so the range is [0, max(byteStart+byteLen)) rather than [min(byteStart), ...). That keeps the request count at one and keeps the run decodable. The same claim is now written into the research corpus at docs/research/30-design-space/04-discovery-and-tailing.md:280-286 ('union its runs into one ranged GET without reading the directory'), which is where a later reader will take it as settled.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.45b implements `direct` by reading ADR-0043 literally: it unions its runs' coordinates into [min(byteStart), max(byteStart+byteLen)) and issues one ranged GET, no directory read, as the record says it may. It works, because every segment today is CODEC_NONE. M2/M10 turns on zstd per run; the consumer now holds compressed bytes with no codecFlags and no way to learn the codec from what it fetched. The repair costs a second request per (node, segment) -- the directory read the coordinates were added to remove -- so the only cost justification recorded for the VERSION_3 bump evaporates, in a record that says 'codec does NOT come back' three paragraphs above the claim.

findings.summary: Grant silently truncates its expiry to milliseconds and the public javadoc never says so, so `new Grant(u, t).expiresAt()` is not `t`; the truncation itself is correct and pinned, but the only statement of it is a // comment inside the compact constructor
findings.detail: The fix is the right one -- truncating at construction makes the in-memory value the one that travels, and SubscriptionEventGrantTest.aSUBMILLISECONDExpirySurvivesTheWire pins both halves. What is missing is the contract: the class javadoc records the redaction and 'THE EXPIRY IS SAFE TO SHOW', and says nothing about precision, so a caller reading the API sees a record component it passed in and gets a different Instant back. The javadoc is where `SignedUrl`-to-`Grant` adapters will be written (M5.45b), and the two types now disagree on precision by design. Second, smaller: the `millis < 0` guard is load-bearing for encode-decode totality in exactly the way the negative byteStart guard was -- without it, `new Grant(url, Instant.ofEpochSecond(-1))` constructs, `SegmentWriter.putUvarint(-1000)` emits a ten-byte varint, and decode's own `expiresAtMillis < 0` check refuses it as 'not an instant'. Nothing constructs a pre-epoch grant in any test (GrantTest covers null/blank url and null expiry; SubscriptionEventGrantTest covers Instant.MAX), so deleting that `if` reintroduces encode-emits-what-decode-refuses with the suite green.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.45b adapts a real presigner: `new Grant(signed.url(), signed.expiresAt())`, where SignedUrl's expiry came from `clock.instant().plus(ttl)` and carries microseconds on Linux. Any assertion or comparison that the grant on the event matches the issuer's own SignedUrl -- `assertThat(event.grant().expiresAt()).isEqualTo(signed.expiresAt())` is the natural way to write the criterion-7 TTL case -- fails by up to 999 microseconds, and the author debugs the wire format looking for a field that is in fact exact. Separately: a future edit deleting `Grant.java`'s `millis < 0` branch (it reads like a redundant defensive check, since the truncation above it cannot make a value negative that was not) leaves a pre-epoch grant encoding to bytes decode refuses, with :format:test green.
